name: Mometasone

card.summary: Potent steroid for allergies, asthma and eczema, with no hair-loss studies found.
card.note: Corticosteroid; topical use on skin is typically short term due to thinning risk.

quick.overview:
Mometasone furoate is a corticosteroid used in nasal sprays, inhalers and skin creams for allergy, asthma and eczema.
Although topical steroids as a class are associated with alopecia areata care, no hair-loss data exist for mometasone itself.
quick.mechanism: It binds glucocorticoid receptors and dampens inflammatory signaling.
quick.risks: Risks listed include local infections, adrenal suppression with heavy exposure, skin thinning with prolonged topical use and fetal risk in animal studies.

lead: Mometasone furoate is a synthetic glucocorticoid anti-inflammatory used in nasal, inhaled and topical forms. Its appearance relevance comes mainly from the topical form (brand name Elocon and generics), which clinicians use on inflammatory skin conditions such as eczema, contact dermatitis and psoriasis, where the aim is calmer, less red and less scaly skin [1][2][8]. Nasal sprays (Nasonex and others) treat allergic rhinitis and nasal polyps, and inhalers (Asmanex) treat asthma [1][2].

People interested in how they look encounter mometasone as a prescription corticosteroid in dermatology, and the wiki lists it because topical corticosteroids are among the treatments associated with inflammatory scalp and skin conditions, including alopecia areata and seborrhoeic dermatitis. Reviews of seborrhoeic dermatitis, a common cause of scalp flaking and facial redness, describe topical corticosteroids among the treatment options [3][4]. No trial of mometasone for hair loss is documented in the material reviewed.

Mometasone furoate was patented in 1981 and came into medical use in 1987; it is on the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines and is sold as a generic [8]. Wikipedia describes it as more potent than hydrocortisone but weaker than dexamethasone, and in 2023 it was prescribed more than 800,000 times in the US [8]. Its safety profile depends on route and duration, with skin thinning a recognised effect of prolonged topical corticosteroid use [1][8].

chain: Calmer, less red, less scaly skin during flares
angle.text: Topical mometasone is a prescription steroid used on inflamed skin such as eczema and psoriasis patches. Appearance benefit comes from reduced redness, scaling and swelling while the flare is treated.

Prescription in most countries; OTC nasal spray product in the US [8]
Marketed as the 17-furoate ester prodrug (C27H30O6Cl2); 98-99% protein-bound[8]

paras: Intranasal mometasone is used for seasonal and perennial allergic rhinitis in adults and children aged 2 and over, and for nasal polyps in adults [1]. A JAMA review of allergic rhinitis notes that the condition affects an estimated 15% of the US population and is associated with asthma, eczema and sinusitis [6]. Inhaled mometasone is indicated as maintenance treatment of asthma in people aged 4 and over [1][2]. Topical mometasone is used for atopic dermatitis, contact dermatitis and psoriasis, typically for short courses [1].
A drug-repurposing review lists mometasone furoate among older drugs screened by academic and small-business groups for new uses.

Topical corticosteroids reduce redness, swelling and scaling in inflammatory skin disease, so people with eczema, psoriasis or seborrhoeic dermatitis on visible areas use them to clear flares [1][3][4]. BMJ Clinical Evidence systematic reviews of seborrhoeic dermatitis, which affects at least 1 to 3 percent of the population by one estimate and notes frequent relapse after treatment, cover topical treatments for the scalp, face and body [3][4]. Mometasone as a specific hair-loss treatment is not documented in published trials in the material reviewed.

In dermatology, mometasone cream has also been studied for skin reactions that are visible to the patient: a double-blind trial found it reduced acute radiation dermatitis in women having breast radiotherapy, and a MASCC guideline recommends prophylactic topical mometasone to reduce discomfort and itching from radiation dermatitis.[15][16]

The US label for inhaled mometasone lists oral Candida infection, immunosuppression, hypercorticism and adrenal suppression, growth effects in children, and glaucoma or cataracts among risks of inhaled corticosteroids, and notes fetal malformations in animal studies [2]. Wikipedia lists headache, sore throat and nosebleeds for the nasal form, and burning, itching, acne, skin atrophy and colour changes for the topical form, with adrenal suppression and slowed growth in children among serious effects [8]. Grokipedia likewise notes that prolonged topical use may thin the skin [1]. A study of nasal mometasone in children with perennial allergic rhinitis found no growth retardation after one year [5].

Mometasone binds glucocorticoid receptors, suppressing inflammatory proteins, increasing anti-inflammatory proteins and reducing inflammatory cell influx [8]. Wikipedia adds that it is a potent progesterone receptor agonist and partial mineralocorticoid agonist [8].

The marketed drug is the furoate ester, a prodrug whose active metabolite is mometasone; protein binding is 98 to 99 percent, elimination half-life is about 5.8 hours, and the liver metabolises it mainly via CYP3A4 [8]. Systemic availability from nasal sprays is barely detectable in plasma, and topical and intranasal use gives low systemic exposure [1][8]. Wikipedia also notes that it inhibits CYP2C8 [8].

Mometasone furoate was patented in 1981 and entered medical use in 1987.[8] It became available in nasal (Nasonex), inhaled (Asmanex) and topical (Elocon) products, plus combinations such as formoterol inhalers and salicylic-acid skin preparations, and later reached generic status and the WHO Essential Medicines List.[8] A 1991 Danish review of the compound and a 2011 drug-repurposing review reflect its long presence in the literature.[1]

Wikipedia reports that mometasone was prescribed more than 800,000 times in the US in 2023, ranking 272nd among medicines [8]. It is prescription-only in Canada and the EU and in the US apart from an OTC nasal spray product; in Australia it is a pharmacy or prescription medicine depending on formulation [8]. Brands include Nasonex, Asmanex and Elocon [8].

Trials registered for mometasone concern respiratory and skin disease, not hair loss. ClinicalTrials.gov entries include a phase 2 study of mometasone nasal spray in 455 people with perennial allergic rhinitis [9], a phase 3 comparison of two dry-powder inhalers in 97 people with asthma [10], a phase 4 comparison of three mometasone furoate products in 32 people with atopic dermatitis [11], and a trial of an asthma and nasal steroid strategy in 388 participants [12]. A 2024 randomised trial compared mometasone nasal spray combined with desloratadine or montelukast in children with allergic rhinitis [13]. The phase 3 IRIDIUM study evaluated a mometasone-containing triple inhaler in asthma [14].

A double-blind randomized study in 49 women with node-negative breast cancer scheduled for postoperative radiotherapy compared mometasone furoate cream plus emollient with emollient alone; the mometasone group had significantly less acute radiation dermatitis (P=0.0033) and pigmentation did not differ.[15]

A multicentre, randomized, placebo-controlled phase III study randomised 98 prepubertal children aged 3 to 9 with perennial allergic rhinitis to mometasone nasal spray or placebo for one year. Heights were similar between groups (gain of 6.95 cm versus 6.35 cm), cosyntropin testing showed no evidence of adrenal suppression, and treatment-related adverse events occurred in 16 percent versus 22 percent.[5] A 2026 randomized trial (MIST+) examined intranasal treatments in children with sleep-disordered breathing.[17]
No studies found for mometasone in alopecia areata or other hair loss.

timeline.event: Paediatric study reports no growth retardation after one year of nasal mometasone [5].
